acts.title: Text A · The left brain, the right brain, and the gap between them
text: In the 1960s a series of experiments was carried out on patients whose two brain hemispheres had been surgically separated. The findings were genuine: the left side does indeed dominate for grammar and logical sequence, whereas the right is better at melody and at recognizing faces.
However, that is where the evidence stops. It does not follow that a person is dominated by one side, and no study has ever found that they are.

Nevertheless, the idea took hold. Psychologists and the press between them came up with the notion of the “right-brained” personality — creative, intuitive, bad with numbers — and self-help books have been converting people from one type to the other ever since.
As a result, hundreds of quizzes pop up the moment you search for the phrase. Not one of them can work out anything at all, because there is nothing to measure.

items.q: What does Text A argue?
o: The original finding was real, but what was built on it is not

items.q: What does “Nevertheless” signal at the start of paragraph three?
o: That what follows contradicts what came before

acts.title: Text B · Why bad ideas survive
text: A false idea survives for three reasons, and being convincing is not one of them.
Firstly, it is useful. “I am right-brained” explains a bad school report at no cost to anybody. Consequently it gets repeated, and repetition is what people mistake for evidence.
Secondly, it is unfalsifiable. If you are told you are creative and you turn out to be good with numbers, that simply makes you unusual. Nothing can ever come along and settle it.

Thirdly — and this is the one that matters — nobody has to sort it out. A false idea about brain hemispheres costs nothing, so no institution is funded to phase it out, whereas a false idea about a medicine gets tested within the year.
In other words, ideas do not survive because they are true. They survive because nothing in particular kills them.

items.s: The writer gives three reasons why false ideas survive.
One reason is that repetition is mistaken for evidence.
The writer says the idea can easily be proved false.
A false idea about medicine is treated differently, according to the text.
The writer concludes that ideas survive because they are true.

acts.title: What is each linker doing?
text: The left side dominates for grammar, whereas the right is better at melody.
However, that is where the evidence stops.
Nevertheless, the idea took hold.
As a result, hundreds of quizzes pop up.
Consequently it gets repeated.
In other words, ideas do not survive because they are true.

items.q: “whereas” signals…
o: a direct contrast between two things

items.q: “However” and “Nevertheless” both signal…
o: that what follows goes against what came before

items.q: “As a result” and “Consequently” both signal…
o: that what follows is caused by what came before

items.q: “In other words” signals…
o: a restatement of the same idea more plainly

acts.title: Out, up, and the shape of a phrasal verb
rule: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle, and the particle usually carries a rough direction of meaning. out tends towards completion or discovery; up tends towards creation, arrival or completeness. Neither is a rule, but both are a useful first guess.
points: find out, work out, turn out, sort out, carry out, phase out, run out.
come up with, make up, set up, turn up, pop up.
Most take an object between verb and particle: sort it out, work it out. A pronoun MUST go in the middle.
come up with and run out of never split: come up with it, not come it up with.
Phrasal verbs are neutral to informal. In a formal report, prefer carry out over do, but prefer discover over find out.
eg: They carried out the research in 2019.
carry out — perform.
I would like to find out more about it.
find out — discover.
It turned out that I had remembered it wrongly.
turn out — prove to be.
We just turned up; there was no need to book.
turn up — arrive.
Lights should sort the problem out.
sort out — separable.
Lights should sort it out.
A pronoun must go in the middle.
They came up with the idea in the 1960s.
come up with — never split.
The theory was largely made up.
make up — invent.
Hundreds of quizzes pop up when you search.
pop up — appear.
We are phasing the cameras out.
phase out — separable.
acts.careful: “Sort out it” is wrong. When the object is a pronoun — it, them, him — it always goes between the verb and the particle: sort it out, work them out, turn it up.

write.q: Write about 180 words on an idea that a lot of people believe and you think is wrong — at work, in your field, or in general. Use at least five phrasal verbs from this lesson, and at least four linkers: one contrast, one result, one addition, and one restatement.
write.model:
A great many people in sales believe that the best salespeople are the most talkative ones, and every manager I have worked for has repeated it.

Where it came from is obvious enough. The people who come up with these rules are usually the ones who were promoted, and the ones who get promoted are the ones nobody forgets. However, that is a fact about visibility rather than about results.

The reason it survives is that nobody has to sort it out. Nobody carries out the study, because doing so would cost a quarter and might annoy somebody senior. Consequently the rule is repeated, and repetition turns out to be quite enough.

What would settle it is unglamorous: take four quarters of data and find out how much of each call the customer was talking. My own guess is that it will turn out to be about seventy per cent. In other words, the quietest people in the room are probably the ones to watch.
